BE PREPARED
Passengers should follow all commands and signals
given by crewmembers. Be ready to assist crewmembers
in an emergency and to follow the guidelines below:
1)
Know where all the exits are on this aircraft. Study
the briefing card and know how to open the exit
closest to you.
Ask a crewmember if you have any
questions about this.
2)
Remember, keep your head down until the aircraft
has come to a complete stop. Don't be tempted to
look up and around until you are certain that the
aircraft is no longer moving.
3)
If an emergency evacuation is necessary and if a
crewmember cannot get to the exit, you may have to
open it.
First, look outside. If fire, water or smoke
could come into the cabin through the exit, don't
open it.
4)
If it is safe to open the exit, do so as quickly as
possible. Keep the pathway clear. If the exit cannot
be opened, go to another exit.
5) When the exit is open, push the door all the way
open and out of the way.
6)
Assess the condition of the escape slide and stabi-
lize it if necessary.
7)
When the exit is opened and the slide is deployed,
shout "Open seatbelts, come this way!" then go out
as quickly as possible.
8)
To use the slide, jump out and away from the aircraft
with your legs out.
Land on the slide on your bottom
in a sitting position.
9)
Assist the people behind you off the end of the slide.
Direct them away from any dangers, such as fire,
smoke or water.
10) Don't take any carry-on baggage with you. It only
gets in the way and impedes the evacuation.
11) Move 300 yards away from the aircraft as soon
and as quickly as you can.
TO SIT IN AN EXIT ROW
In order to ensure the fastest possible emergency evacuation, the
Federal Aviation Administration has set standards for people who sit
in rows next to exits.
In the event of an emergency, these passen-
gers may be called upon to assist crewmembers in the evacuation.
Passengers sitting in exit row seats must be willing and able
to do the following:
1)
Locate the emergency exit and move quickly to it;
2)
Recognize the opening mechanism, comprehend the instruc-
tions, then open the exit at the proper time;
3)
Decide if opening the exit will increase hazards to passengers;
4)
Follow instructions given by crewmembers;
5)
Stow the exit doors;
6)
Pass quickly through the door and then assess, select and
follow a safe path away from the aircraft.
In order to perform all these functions, passengers sitting in
emergency exit rows must:
1) Read English well enough to understand the instructions for
opening exits and for other emergency procedures;
2)
See well enough to read instructions, to see signals given by
crewmembers
and to look outside
TOr
dangers
such
smoke, fire or water which would make the exit unusable. You
can wear glasses or contact lenses;
Hear well enough to understand English commands. You can
use a hearing aid;
4) Speak well
enough to give information in English to
crewmembers or other passengers during an emergency;
5)
Be able to use both hands, both arms and both legs, as well
as be strong and flexible enough to do the following:
a. Be able to quickly open the exit. This will require that you
be able to reach up, sideways and down and be able to
grasp the door mechanism;
b. Be able to lift the exit door out of the exit and over a row
of seats; some window hatches that must be lifted can
weigh as much as 65 pounds (30 Kgs.), the average
weight of a 7 year old child;
c. Be able to clear from the exit any obstructions weighing up
to 65 pounds and to maintain balance while doing so;
d. Be able to quickly move to and through the exit;
e. Be able to help other passengers away from the plane;
6) Be at least 15 years of age;
7) Have the capacity to perform
these functions without a
companion or adult;
8) Be with no one that requires your care, such as a small child,
someone physically or mentally unable
to care for
themselves;
9) You must be willing and able to do all of these things by
yourself and without harming yourself.
If you cannot or do not wish to do all these things, you cannot sit
in an emergency exit row seat. If you are already seated there,
ask a crewmember to move you to another seat. You do not have
to explain why. You need to say only, "I do not want to sit in an exit row."
PORTABLE ELECTRONIC
DEVICES
Atlantic Southeast Airlines
and
the Federal Aviation
Administration restrict the use of certain portable elec-
tronic devices on board the aircraft, as they can interfere
with the navigation and communication systems on the
aircraft.
Please be certain that all devices are in the
"OFF" position during taxi, take off and landing.
The following devices are permitted only at cruise altitude
when the Captain has turned off the seatbelt sign. They
should be turned off at all other times:
The following devices may not be used at any time on
the aircraft:
Personal computers and computer games
VHF scanner receivers
Tape players that do not have AM/FM capability
Video recorders
Calculators
Cellular telephones
Two-way radios (CB, Ham, or Walkie Talkie)
49 MHz transmitters
Remote controlled toys
External computer devices,
such
as mouse, joy
stick, or printer
AM/FM radios or TV's
Compact disc players
Any other device which the crew suspects may
interfere with the aircraft systems
Passengers must comply with all crewmember instructions.
Atlantic Southeast Airlines appreciates your cooperation.
